IV SOI spin splitting in machine learning-optimized Si bumps

V Additional data on Si-spikes Ge+

V.1 Manual optimization

In this section we report additional simulation results on the manually optimized Si-spikes. In Fig. 3 we show the variation of Δ 1 against the spikes distances d 1 , 2 at gate field F z = 1.5 ​ mV / nm . We also show in panel (b) and (c) the SOI strength β 2 against F z and l z respectively.

We also report the variation of β 2 (Fig. 4 ) and the LH-HH splitting energy (Fig. 5 ) with respect to d 1 and d 2 for various gate field strengths, other than the one presented in the main article.

In Fig. 6 we show the ground state and first excited state (which is LH-like) wave function of the machine learning-optimized Ge+, corresponding to the system in the 3 rd column of Table 1 in the main text.

VI Andreev spin qubits

VI.1 Linearized model of Andreev spin qubits

We study the non-interacting model for an Andreev Spin Qubit (ASQ), looking at a general equation for the spin-splitting in terms of Fermi velocities of up and down spins.
We consider a single ASQ first in a 1D SNS junction with 3 regions for z < − L / 2 , | z | < L / 2 , and z > L / 2 described by the three Hamiltonians, respectively

H L = ( ℏ ​ v L ​ k z − μ ) ​ τ z + Δ L ​ ( e − i ​ φ L ​ τ + + e i ​ φ L ​ τ − ) , (67) H N = [ ℏ ​ ( v + σ z ​ δ ​ v / 2 ) ​ k z − μ ] ​ τ z (68) H R = ( ℏ ​ v R ​ k z − μ ) ​ τ z + Δ R ​ ( e − i ​ φ R ​ τ + + e i ​ φ R ​ τ − ) . (69)

Here we consider a linearized Hamiltonian close to the chemical potential μ ≫ Δ m = L , R of the different regions with ⟨ z | k z = − i ∂ z ⟨ z | and τ i acting on the Nambu space. Each Hamiltonian above has its respective copy at opposite momentum with negative velocities. We do not include Zeeman fields, but we include a possible difference in Fermi velocities from the up and down spins δ ​ v due to SOI. The velocity v is the average velocity at the given μ , and we anticipate that it can differ from the velocity without SOI.

The Hamiltonians H L and H R are independent of the spin σ and can be diagonalized only within a given spin subspace without loss of generality. The eigenvalue problem then reduces to a 2 × 2 problem in Nambu space ( m = L , R ):

[ ℏ ​ v m ​ k z − μ Δ m ​ e − i ​ φ m Δ m ​ e i ​ φ m − ℏ ​ v m ​ k z + μ ] ​ [ | ψ m ↑ ⟩ | ψ m ↓ ⟩ ] = ϵ ​ [ | ψ m ↑ ⟩ | ψ m ↓ ⟩ ] , (70)

where ↑ , ↓ refer to the up and down Nambu component, respectively. This Hamiltonian has the general solution:

ψ m ↑ ​ ( z ) = Δ m e − i φ m / 2 e i ​ z / ξ m ( C e − z / l m ϵ − i ​ Γ m + D ​ e z / l m ϵ + i ​ Γ m ) , (71a) ψ m ↓ ​ ( z ) = e i ​ φ m / 2 e i ​ z / ξ m ( C e − z / l m + D e z / l m ) , (71b)

where Γ m = Δ m 2 − ϵ 2 , ξ m = ℏ ​ v m / μ and l m = ℏ ​ v m / Γ m . The coefficients C and D are arbitrary constants. We restrict ourselves to bound states, and thus we require the wavefunctions to vanish at infinity, and in the left (right) region we impose C = 0 ( D = 0 ). Reintroducing the spin degree of freedom, we have the total solutions for the left and right regions

| ψ L ⟩ = ∫ d ​ z ​ | z ⟩ ​ [ | ↑ ⟩ ​ ψ L ↑ ​ ( z ) + | ↓ ⟩ ​ ψ L ↓ ​ ( z ) ] ​ ( α ​ | + ⟩ + β ​ | − ⟩ ) , (72) | ψ R ⟩ = ∫ d ​ z ​ | z ⟩ ​ [ | ↑ ⟩ ​ ψ R ↑ ​ ( z ) + | ↓ ⟩ ​ ψ R ↓ ​ ( z ) ] ​ ( γ ​ | + ⟩ + δ ​ | − ⟩ ) , (73)

where α , β , γ and δ are arbitrary constants and

ψ L ↑ ​ ( z ) = Δ L ϵ + i ​ Γ L e − i φ L / 2 e i ​ z / ξ L e z / l L , (75) ψ R ↑ ​ ( z ) = Δ R ϵ − i ​ Γ R e − i φ R / 2 e i ​ z / ξ R e − z / l R , (76) ψ L ↓ ​ ( z ) = e i ​ φ L / 2 ​ e i ​ z / ξ L ​ e z / l L , (77) ψ R ↓ ​ ( z ) = e i ​ φ R / 2 e i ​ z / ξ R e − z / l R . (78)

Here we absorbed the C and D constants into α ​ … ​ δ .

In the semiconductor, the Hamiltonian is diagonal in both Nambu and spin space. The general solution for Nambu component τ = ↑ , ↓ and spin component σ = + , − is

[ ℏ ​ ( v + σ ​ δ ​ v / 2 ) ​ k z − μ ] ​ τ ​ | ψ N τ ​ σ ⟩ = ϵ ​ | ψ N τ ​ σ ⟩ (79) ⇔ ψ N τ ​ σ ​ ( z ) = ⟨ z | ψ N τ ​ σ ⟩ = e i ​ z / ξ N σ ​ e i ​ τ ​ z / l N σ , (80)

where ξ N σ = ℏ ​ v σ / μ , l N σ = ℏ ​ v σ / ϵ and v σ = v + σ ​ δ ​ v / 2 . A total general state for the semiconducting region is therefore

| ψ N ⟩ = a ​ | ↑ ⟩ ​ | + ⟩ ​ | ψ N ↑ ⁣ + ⟩ + b ​ | ↑ ⟩ ​ | − ⟩ ​ | ψ N ↑ ⁣ − ⟩ + c ​ | ↓ ⟩ ​ | + ⟩ ​ | ψ N ↓ ⁣ + ⟩ + d ​ | ↓ ⟩ ​ | − ⟩ ​ | ψ N ↓ ⁣ − ⟩ , (81)

with a , b , c and d arbitrary constants. If we neglect any flipping of the spin upon reflection at the superconducting-semiconducting interfaces, then we can discard the spin-down components of the total wavefunction, and solve the simultaneous boundary conditions only for the | ↑ ⟩ ​ | + ⟩ and | ↓ ⟩ ​ | + ⟩ components. This is equivalent to setting β = δ = 0 and b = d = 0 and gives the following four continuity conditions at | z | = L / 2 :

γ ​ ψ R ↑ ​ ( L 2 ) = a ​ ψ N ↑ ⁣ + ​ ( L 2 ) , γ ​ ψ R ↓ ​ ( L 2 ) = c ​ ψ N ↓ ⁣ + ​ ( L 2 ) , (82) α ​ ψ L ↑ ​ ( − L 2 ) = a ​ ψ N ↑ ⁣ + ​ ( − L 2 ) , α ​ ψ L ↓ ​ ( − L 2 ) = c ​ ψ N ↓ ⁣ + ​ ( − L 2 ) . (83)

From Eqs. ( 82 ) and ( 83 ) we obtain, respectively

a c = Δ R ϵ − i ​ Γ R e − i ​ φ R e − i L / l N + , (84) a c = Δ L ϵ + i ​ Γ L ​ e − i ​ φ L ​ e i ​ L / l N + , (85)

which leads to the general solution for ϵ , assuming Δ R = Δ L = Δ :

ϵ ​ sin ⁡ ( ϵ / E L − φ / 2 ) = Δ 2 − ϵ 2 ​ cos ⁡ ( ϵ / E L − φ / 2 ) , (86)

where E L = ℏ ​ v + / L and φ = φ L − φ R . The same equation also holds for the spin-down level with v + replaced by v − , and agrees with Reference 6 in the short junction limit at perfect transparency. Taking the square followed by an arccos function on both sides of ( 86 ) leads to the alternative formulation [ 7 ] :

arccos ⁡ ( ϵ Δ ) − ϵ E L = − φ 2 + n ​ π , (87)

where n is an integer.
